summary: Geoffrey Delamayn thanks the lady who picked him for croquet but asks her to choose someone else, saying the game is not in his line. Such a reply would once have seemed rude, but the company now finds it amusing and laughs. Blanche loses her temper and asks sharply whether he cares for anything besides rowing and jumping. She mocks him for having muscles instead of a mind. Her sharp words have no effect on him at all.

Lady Lundie, wanting to win favour with her brother-in-law, surprises everyone by choosing Sir Patrick as her second croquet player. Blanche protests that her uncle will never play, since croquet did not exist in his day. Sir Patrick replies that people once had to bring agreeable qualities to social gatherings, while now a mallet and a ball are enough. He picks them up and agrees to play. To the amazement of the younger guests, he lays his hand on his heart and prepares to quote Dryden to Lady Lundie.

Arnold, who knows little of life on shore after his years at sea, fails to take Sir Patrick's joke and blushes irritably. Sir Patrick rewards himself for his clever reply with a pinch of snuff from his ivory cane. Blanche then arrives, tells Arnold she will need him soon, and reminds her uncle that it is his turn to play. Sir Patrick, who had forgotten the game, rolls his ball onto the lawn and tucks his mallet under his arm like an umbrella. As he hobbles out, he muses that the most serious question left to him in old age is whether he will get through the hoops.

In the summer-house, Arnold tells Blanche he would like a little encouragement. Blanche glances back, since the players on the lawn below could be heard and might come up at any moment. The sounds of the game suggest Sir Patrick has been allowed a second try, which gives the couple a few more seconds. Arnold seizes the moment, speaks his feelings, and takes her hand. Although Blanche had longed to hear his confession, she now struggles to free her hand and asks him to let her go.

Blanche tells Arnold to go and make sure he gets through the hoop, with her hands on his shoulders and her face close to his. Arnold catches her round the waist and kisses her, leaving her speechless. Hearing footsteps approaching, he gives her a last squeeze and runs out. Blanche opens her eyes to find Anne Silvester standing alone and looking at her. She throws her arms around Anne and whispers that Arnold has proposed and is hers for life.

Anne knocks the pipe out of Geoffrey's hand in fury and calls his conduct infamous, daring him to defend it. He makes no defence and instead worries about his pipe, which had cost him ten shillings. He picks it up, finds it unbroken, and puts it away with relief. Then, calm and relaxed, he tells her there is no point in bullying him. He warns her that she does not want the people on the lawn to hear, and complains that women never learn prudence.

Anne tells Geoffrey that she will go where many miserable women have gone before her, out of the world, meaning she will kill herself. Geoffrey studies her closely and realises she truly means it. Frightened and angry, he pushes a chair towards her with his foot and roughly orders her to sit down. She obeys but sits in silence, determined and indifferent to how things end. He paces the summer-house, then strikes the rail of her chair and demands to know what she wants.

Geoffrey forces Anne back into the chair before the people at the game can hear her. He tells her he will do what she wants if she is reasonable, but insists he cannot marry her that day because the house is full of guests. Anne says it can be done and that she has a plan she has been thinking about since they arrived. Cursing her stubbornness, he finally agrees to hear it. Anne, now hopeful, raises her hand for silence and listens to make sure nobody is coming up from the lawn.

Worn out by Geoffrey's brutal indifference and Lady Lundie's petty malice, Anne leaves the summer-house before she breaks down in tears. Lady Lundie appeals to Sir Patrick, but he simply bows, takes snuff, and goes on watching the lawn-party. Before Lady Lundie can press him further, Arnold and Blanche arrive at the foot of the steps. Sir Patrick asks when the dancing will begin, and Blanche asks whether Anne is feeling better. Lady Lundie answers that Miss Silvester has gone to her room and remarks scornfully that such half-bred people are always rude when they are ill.

Sir Patrick teases Arnold for looking so serious and asks whether he is about to appeal to him as head of the family. Arnold, sensing this would put Sir Patrick off, carefully reminds him that he had promised a private talk before Arnold left Windygates. Sir Patrick agrees and offers his worldly experience, but warns Arnold not to treat him as head of the family, since he has resigned that role to Lady Lundie. Arnold is unsure how to raise the subject of Blanche without provoking Sir Patrick's wit. He makes a poor start by hesitating.

A shadow falls across the summer-house steps, and a groom in riding livery appears. He is a stranger to the place and says he has come from the house of Julius Delamayn, Geoffrey's brother. He carries an urgent message and a card that his master wants delivered to Geoffrey at once. He asks the two gentlemen whether they know where Geoffrey is. Arnold says he has not seen him and asks Sir Patrick if he has.

Geoffrey is relieved to learn that the urgent news is not about his horse Ratcatcher but about his father. The groom explains that a telegram has come from London with bad news of Lord Holchester. Julius's card says their father is dangerously ill, his lawyer has been sent for, and Geoffrey should meet him at the junction to take the first train to London. Geoffrey silently checks his watch, since Anne had told him to wait half an hour for word from her. No word has come, which means Anne has safely left the house and is on her way to the mountain inn.

Arnold pleads that he cannot leave without saying goodbye to Blanche. Sir Patrick smiles and points to the steps, where Blanche has followed him from the house. Arnold runs to her and whispers that he will be back in two days and that Sir Patrick has given his consent. Blanche holds his arm, unhappy with such a rushed parting, until Geoffrey literally tears Arnold away. Once they vanish into the shrubbery, Blanche angrily asks her uncle why that brute is taking Arnold with him.

Sir Patrick finds he must take charge at Windygates. Lady Lundie has resolved to track Anne down and find out whether she is really married. Blanche, after a fit of hysterical tears, is sure Anne is in some terrible trouble, since Anne would never have hidden a marriage from her or written such a formal goodbye, and she too wants to follow and help her. Sir Patrick sees that both women could do something very rash unless they are restrained, and admits that he is the man to do it. Pacing the garden, he grumbles to his servant Simpson about the burdens married friends put on a bachelor, then decides to see Lady Lundie first.

At the inn, Anne is startled to notice an old man quietly dusting the furniture in the parlour. He has one blind eye and one merry eye, a bald head, gouty feet, and a famously large red nose. He combines servility with independence, and great impudence and cunning with dry humour, and no amount of whisky ever makes him drunk. He is Bishopriggs, the headwaiter of the Craig Fernie Inn and the right-hand man of the landlady, Mistress Inchbare. When Anne sharply asks what he is doing, he says he is tidying the room for her and then points meaningfully at the purse in her hand.

Anne looks out of the window and sees that the weather has turned grey and cloudy. As she tries to rest on the sofa, she hears voices and footsteps in the passage. Fearing they might be strangers, since the landlady has refused to let her keep the rooms, she runs into the bedroom and locks herself in. Bishopriggs then shows Arnold Brinkworth into the sitting room. Arnold asks where she is, and Bishopriggs points to the bedroom, saying his good lady is surely in there.

Anne struggles to compose herself and tells Arnold that he comforts her and that crying does her good. She thanks him and admits she had thought he was like other men until she saw how kind he could be. Changing the subject, she asks if he walked there and offers him whatever the inn can provide. Arnold, moved by her situation, says he only wants to be of service. He asks if there is anything he can do to make her more comfortable and urges her to stay, since Geoffrey wishes it.

Arnold explains that Geoffrey told him Anne's position at the inn depended on Arnold asking for her at the door as her husband. He points out that if he had asked for her only as a friend, the landlady would surely have made more trouble about the rooms. Anne knows he is right and that the deception was made necessary by her own situation, since she could not have foreseen Geoffrey leaving for London. Still, she feels uneasy and afraid of what might happen next, and she sits twisting her handkerchief without answering. Arnold assures her he does not mind the trick, since he is serving his old friend and helping the woman who will soon be Geoffrey's wife.

Anne begs Arnold to leave her to her solitude and sorrow and says goodbye. Arnold asks what she is afraid of, but she cannot fully put her fears into words. Searching for a reason that will make him go, she asks him to imagine Blanche hearing about what he has done, since the longer he stays the more likely it is that she will. Arnold does not believe Blanche would be angry at him for helping her. Anne insists that she understands Blanche better and again begs him to go, saying she does not like his coming there at all.

Bishopriggs points out a cloud coming up the valley against the wind and warns that a storm is brewing. The landlady, Mistress Inchbare, then knocks and comes in, speaking only to Arnold. She says she was not there when he arrived and must now ask whether he is taking the rooms for himself and the lady as his wife. Anne raises her head to speak, but Arnold presses her hand under the table to silence her. He answers that he certainly takes the rooms for himself and this lady, his wife.

Anne is too upset to finish her sentence, so Arnold makes her drink a glass of wine and patiently defends what he did. He asks whether he should have let the landlady shut the door on her with a storm coming and nowhere else to go. He says that her scruples are out of place with such a woman and that he is responsible to Geoffrey for her safety. He then drinks to Blanche's health, calling the sherry the weakest he has ever tasted. When Bishopriggs arrives with the water, Arnold mockingly asks if he used it all on the sherry, and Bishopriggs stops in shocked amazement.

Bishopriggs whistles in surprise at the way Arnold talks about the nuptial chamber and directs him to another room down the passage, and Arnold hurries out. Thinking the pair have eloped against Sir Patrick's wishes, Bishopriggs tells Anne it is bad business to deceive Sir Patrick, mentioning that he once worked as a clerk in Sir Patrick's chambers in Edinburgh. The landlady calls him away before he can say more. Left alone at the window, Anne realises that her hiding place has been discovered at Windygates and wonders whether Sir Patrick comes as a friend or an enemy. Before she can decide what to do, Bishopriggs shows Sir Patrick into the sitting room.

Bishopriggs lectures Arnold on the expense women cause men, including the cost of separation, whether settled amicably or in court. Arnold loses patience and turns to the door. Bishopriggs then tells him that Sir Patrick has left and the lady is alone and waiting for him. Arnold anxiously asks Anne if there is bad news from Lady Lundie's house. Anne finishes addressing a letter to Blanche and tells him it was only a warning that they have found out at Windygates where she is.

Anne insists that Arnold must leave, but he points out that his home is a long journey away by rail and that the train has already gone. As thunder and lightning come closer and rain beats on the window, he sits down, determined to stay. He argues that no one would give him horses in such weather and that they could not cross the moor anyway. Anne protests that his staying the night after what he told the landlady would put them in a cruelly embarrassing position. Arnold, unaware he has said anything to offend her, sees no difficulty, since she has the bedroom and he can sleep on the sofa as he has slept in far worse places at sea.

Bishopriggs sits over his whisky toddy and ignores the bell that keeps ringing for him. He grumbles that Sir Patrick spoiled the dinner by arriving at the start of it and that the young gentleman is greedy and knows nothing about wine, still smarting over the watered sherry. Meanwhile the lightning and thunder grow closer over the moor. Just as Arnold is about to ring a fourth time, a knock comes at the door. Following his own fixed habit, Bishopriggs knocks a second time before entering with the untouched dish of collops.

Blanche has arrived at the inn, and Anne coldly says she cannot talk about her troubles yet. Anne reminds Blanche that she promised her uncle to stay at Windygates and asks why she came that night. Blanche says she knew something was wrong, because Anne would never have hidden her marriage from her or left such a cold letter. She demands to know why Anne's husband made her leave so suddenly and why he slipped out of the room in the dark as if afraid to be seen. Just then Mistress Inchbare returns with some clothes, and Anne gladly takes the candles and leads the way into the bedroom.

Anne comes close to telling Blanche the truth but stops herself at the last moment. She cannot explain why Arnold joined her at Craig Fernie without confessing her shameful situation with Geoffrey, which would damage Arnold in Blanche's eyes and cause a scandal at the inn. She decides that Blanche must be kept in ignorance and Arnold must stay hidden until she leaves. Meanwhile Blanche is eagerly asking Mistress Inchbare to describe Anne's invisible husband. Afraid of what the landlady might say, Anne quickly sends her away, saying she will help Miss Lundie herself.

In London, the butler explains that Lord Holchester suffered a paralytic stroke and that the doctors had given him up when Lady Holchester telegraphed. However, the lord's health has now improved, which puts Geoffrey in an awkward position. Geoffrey had been forbidden to enter the house, and his only excuse for coming was that his father was dying. The servants, the butler, and Julius all look at one another in an uncomfortable silence. Geoffrey tells the footmen to open the door and says he is leaving.

Unable to make up his mind about writing a letter, Geoffrey decides to clear his head with an elaborate bath involving steam, cold water, and massage. He returns to his hotel refreshed, but the indecision soon comes back, and he blames Anne for it. He then works out furiously with heavy dumb-bells until his spirits rise and he swears cheerfully. Declaring his mind made up, he writes and finishes the letter, but at the last minute he reads it again and tears it up. Bewildered, he declares he is out of his mind and sends for Crouch.

Lord Holchester asks Julius to make a note of the name Anne Silvester. He says her parents are dead, that he knew her father, and that her mother was badly treated, which he has been thinking about for the first time in years. He tells Julius to help the girl if she ever asks for help. He then impatiently asks about Julius's election campaign, saying his mind needs something to do. After hearing the report, he blames Lady Holchester for calling Julius to London when he should be addressing the voters.

A servant warns Geoffrey not to show himself at the front of the house because the excited crowd might get out of hand, so he agrees to leave by the back. Alone, he considers what stands between him and the fortune his brother has offered. The Sports are no problem, since the committee will delay the race and a month of training will be enough. He has no objection to courting Mrs Glenarm, as long as his father is satisfied and the money is right. The only real obstacle is Anne, the woman he has ruined.

Arnold advises Geoffrey to consult Sir Patrick, who has spent his life practising Scottish law, and suggests he present it as a friend's case without naming names. Geoffrey likes the idea and tries to leave the library to find Sir Patrick at once. Arnold stops him again with more questions. He points out that Geoffrey cannot go to the hotel as Anne's husband, because Arnold has already taken that role. He asks how Geoffrey plans to meet Anne, who is alone and weary of waiting, and whether he can see her that day.

Arnold admits he is out of sorts that morning and has an uneasy feeling he cannot explain. Geoffrey scoffs that the problem is not his mind but his body, since he is nearly a stone overweight. He tells Arnold to sweat it off with dumb-bells and running uphill in a greatcoat. As Geoffrey tries a third time to leave the library, a servant arrives with a letter and says the messenger is waiting for an answer. Geoffrey sees it is from his brother Julius, whom he had left at the junction three hours earlier, and wonders what he could want.

While Arnold reads Paradise Lost aloud, Blanche suddenly throws off her handkerchief and tells him to stop. She says the words about that happy state make her think of marriage, and marriage reminds her of Anne. She then tells him what she asked Sir Patrick about how Anne's husband had wronged her. Sir Patrick thought it might be connected with the marriage, since private marriages are dangerous, especially in Scotland. He suggested that if they married in Scotland, Anne might doubt whether her marriage was valid at all.

Blanche tells Arnold that Anne has not answered her letter, even though she begged for a single line saying whether she and Sir Patrick had guessed Anne's trouble correctly. She fears that the wickedness of the man who blew out the candles may be worse than they imagined, and she will not bear the doubt beyond that day. Arnold's heart sinks as he senses a new complication. Blanche whispers that Anne may come to see her privately during luncheon, and that Geoffrey at the writing table must not hear. If Anne does not come or send word, Blanche says, Arnold must clear up the mystery himself.

Geoffrey has not been listening, so Arnold tells him again what happened at the inn. Geoffrey listens silently, balancing a paper-knife on his finger and seeming strangely sluggish. Arnold shakes him and says that Geoffrey must now get him out of his difficulty with Blanche by settling things with Anne that day. Geoffrey finally looks up and says Arnold may consider the marriage settled. Arnold offers his hand in congratulation, but Geoffrey ignores it and stares out of the window.

In a library debate, Sir Patrick argues that outdoor life and physical strength do not produce good character. He points out that agricultural labourers and merchant sailors lead outdoor lives, yet the worst crimes are committed in country districts rather than in the towns. He suggests Arnold, who served in the merchant navy, could say what kind of moral example the English sailor is. Geoffrey's friends protest that they are neither labourers nor sailors. Geoffrey sits staring blankly ahead, until he finally challenges Sir Patrick to name the ruthless man he has been describing.

A surgeon tells Geoffrey he noticed that Geoffrey stayed silent during the argument, letting his friends speak for him until something irritated him. He explains that as a doctor he sometimes needs to understand people's minds to understand their bodies. He then raises a physical objection to the craze for athletics, alongside Sir Patrick's moral one. From his own experience, he says that many young men are permanently damaging their health through violent athletic contests. The public sees only the winners, he adds, while many families in England are left caring for sons broken by the strain.

The surgeon tries to move away, but Geoffrey forces him back to the subject. Geoffrey says he will soon start training for the foot race at Fulham and asks whether the surgeon thinks he will break down. The surgeon says he may possibly get through the race, but hints at consequences. Geoffrey adds that he has agreed to row in the University race next spring. Pulling out his betting book, he challenges the surgeon to back his opinion and offers a hundred pounds that he will be fit to row.

Arnold takes Geoffrey's bet on the surgeon's side, then feels guilty about betting against his friend's health. He assures Geoffrey that he only took the bet to please him, but Geoffrey says a bet is a bet. Geoffrey pulls Arnold aside and asks whether he has annoyed Sir Patrick too much to consult him about the Scottish marriage. He glances slyly across the room as he asks. The surgeon is looking at prints, the ladies are writing invitations, and Sir Patrick is alone at the bookshelves reading.

Sir Patrick declines to walk in the garden because of his lame foot, so Geoffrey leads him towards a curtained recess in the library. Sir Patrick asks whether Geoffrey has come to the right person, and Geoffrey says the problem belongs to a friend who has got into trouble with a woman in Scotland. The friend does not know whether he is married to her or not. Surprisingly, Sir Patrick readily agrees to help and leads the way into the recess himself. His sharp lawyer's mind has linked Geoffrey's request with Blanche's worries about Anne, and he suspects a connection.

Sir Patrick reads through the facts of the case and asks questions about them. Geoffrey explains that the man asked for the lady as his wife at the inn door and said at dinner, in front of the landlady and waiter, that he was taking the rooms for his wife. He insists this was done in earnest and that the man later left on the excuse of business. When asked how long the couple had been in Scotland, Geoffrey recalls that both Anne and Arnold had been there well over three weeks, Arnold having had business in Edinburgh about his inheritance. He tells Sir Patrick they had been in Scotland more than twenty-one days and asks if he will be finished soon.

Sir Patrick had first suspected that Geoffrey was really talking about himself, but as a lawyer he distrusts first impressions. By setting a careful trap, he concludes that Geoffrey is probably describing someone else. He also concludes that Geoffrey has some interest in being sure his friend is legally married under Scottish law. His next tasks are to find out who the lady is and whether she is Anne Silvester. Meanwhile he explains the law honestly but warns Geoffrey not to jump to conclusions, which makes Geoffrey's face cloud over.

Geoffrey presses Sir Patrick about what would happen if his friend wanted to marry another lady, and Sir Patrick privately concludes that Geoffrey's interest is not honest. A servant then mentions the groom who brought a note from Julius that morning. Geoffrey rereads his brother's letter, which asks him to come the next day to help receive Mrs Glenarm. He knows that staying means keeping his promise to Anne, while going means abandoning her on the false pretext that she is Arnold's wife. He writes back to Julius in one line that he will come the next day.

Geoffrey feels no remorse about his scheme, only impatience to reach his goal. The narrator explains that remorse comes from self-respect and respect for others, which the natural man lacks, and Geoffrey is the natural man. When the idea first came to him, its daring startled him, but he soon grew used to it and saw only its practical difficulties. The cruelty and treachery of betraying Arnold never entered his mind. The narrator compares him to a dog that saves a man from drowning and later attacks him, adding that Arnold had simply irritated him.

Geoffrey, having worked through the big difficulties of his plan, cannot solve a small one and grows dizzy walking round and round a tree. He turns away to think about something else and lets his mind drift to the foot race and his training. He then notices a woman, apparently a servant, gathering herbs beyond a row of pear trees. A slate hangs by a string at her side, which puzzles him. Looking for a distraction, he decides to tease her about it.

For the first time in his life, Geoffrey becomes alarmed about himself after a strange impression left by a crazy old woman. He wonders whether it is linked to the broken health the surgeon described, or whether he has simply smoked too much and gone without his usual ale after travelling all night. He leaves the garden to test that theory, looking haggard and anxious. Back in the grounds, he finds a footman and asks for the butler. When the butler stares, Geoffrey demands his old ale and some bread and cheese.

Sir Patrick jokingly warns Blanche that wanting to know things is dangerous, citing Eve and Faust. Blanche insists that he is anxious about something and that he behaved strangely earlier. She says she saw him go off to a private corner with Geoffrey Delamayn while she was writing Lady Lundie's dinner invitations. Sir Patrick teases her about whether that counts as work. Blanche asks what he and Geoffrey could possibly have to discuss and why he now has a worried wrinkle between his eyebrows.

Sir Patrick admits he should not help, since Blanche disobeyed him by going to the inn, but he offers to drive towards Craig Fernie alone in her little carriage in case he meets Anne. Blanche throws her arm round his neck and whispers a very long message for Anne, and Sir Patrick thinks Anne must have noble qualities to inspire such devotion. Separately, a servant named Roberts tells Lady Lundie that the cook seems troubled and worn out and wants the rest of the day off. Lady Lundie dismisses this as nonsense and calls the cook obstinate and idle. She says Hester Dethridge is already under notice and will get no reference if she neglects her duty, and asks who would cook the dinner if she went out.

Blanche is alarmed by Anne's appearance and asks what has happened to her. She reassures Anne that no one will disturb them because everyone is at lunch and the servants are at dinner. Anne silently kisses her in a dull, slow way, without a tear or a sigh. Blanche says Anne must be tired and promises she will not walk back. Anne finally speaks, in a voice that is low and sad but still gentle and lovely.

Anne asks Blanche to list the gentlemen staying in the house, and Blanche fears that her friend's mind has given way. Blanche mentions that Arnold and his hateful friend Geoffrey Delamayn came back that morning. Anne realises that Geoffrey has only just returned from London and has had little time to contact her at the inn, so there is no real reason yet to think he has deserted her. This first hope in four days makes her tremble, flush, and then turn pale. Blanche sees that she urgently needs something to revive her.

Anne steadies herself against the table, giddy and unable to think. Geoffrey tells her he has had a lawyer's advice, but she seems not to hear and keeps vaguely asking what she did at the inn. She comes close and lays her hand on his arm, and he pulls himself free of her dress. As she lies on the floor, he says the word Done. He is then startled by light footsteps hurrying across the hall through a library door left ajar.

The cook, Hester Dethridge, writes on her slate that Anne was brought to this state by a man and that God should be left to take her. Blanche is outraged and calls her horrid, but, frightened by Anne's deep faint, begs Hester to help. Hester submits, signs to Blanche to loosen Anne's dress, and kneels to support Anne while it is done. Anne shudders, her eyelids flicker, and she lets out a faint sigh, and Hester writes that the shiver means someone walked over her grave. Horrified, Blanche asks Hester to leave them.

Blanche urges Anne to confide in Sir Patrick, praising him as the wisest and kindest man and saying he had planned to visit her at the inn. She presses for a simple yes or no, and Anne agrees. Delighted, Blanche explains her plan. She will go in to lunch and quietly tell Sir Patrick, who will slip away and take Anne to the summer-house. She will follow once she has satisfied Lady Lundie, and nobody but the three of them will know.

At lunch, Lady Lundie presses Sir Patrick to try her cake. He escapes with a gallant compliment, saying that a wise man flees from temptation he cannot resist. Knowing Lady Lundie will soon leave the table too, he hurries to the library as fast as his lame foot allows. Alone, he looks anxious and grave. He finds the library empty, with no sign of Anne, and says this looks bad.

Sir Patrick gently warns Blanche to prepare for a disappointment, telling her he is alone and never saw Anne. Blanche rushes into the summer-house, then comes out in despair, saying she pitied Anne and Anne has shown her no pity. Sir Patrick asks her not to judge Anne harshly, since some serious necessity may excuse her. He suggests Anne trusts nobody and only agreed to see him to spare Blanche a painful parting. He tells Blanche he has hopes of finding where Anne has gone if she will help him.

Sir Patrick explains that Scottish peasants would never reveal that Anne was sheltering with them without her permission. He argues they should think about what Anne plans to do next, which is surely to leave the area as soon as possible. Since she is not strong, she must either hire a carriage or take the train, so he decides to go to the station first. Blanche says the next train is in half an hour and Anne cannot reach it in time. Sir Patrick replies that she may have help, perhaps even from a husband, and insists on hurrying to the station.

Sir Patrick points to two events at the inn: Anne lost a letter there, and Bishopriggs has quarrelled with Mrs Inchbare and left his job. He says the letter, whether lost or stolen, might help them discover something if they can find it. He then reveals that Bishopriggs once worked as a clerk in his chambers and is an intelligent but unscrupulous old rogue. He was honest about money but would break a trust whenever it served him without breaking the law. Sir Patrick dismissed him after finding he had a copy of his seal and suspecting him of tampering with clients' papers.

Sir Patrick praises Blanche's grasp of mind and jokes that she will rule her household while Arnold will be a constitutional husband. He promises to tell her everything when he returns. He checks that his servant Duncan has the bag and the timetable, and lets Duncan drive so he can think. He then calls for them to go to the station. The chaise rattles out of the gates, Sir Patrick waves as he turns the corner, and Blanche is left alone in the yard.

Blanche passes on Sir Patrick's instructions about the crossroads and the need for secrecy, and Arnold agrees to help and keep the secret. Sitting on the heather by a farmhouse with a cigar, he puzzles over why Anne came to Windygates and then fled. He assumes Geoffrey had gone to meet Anne and that the two must have missed each other, but he cannot guess why she ran away. After half an hour he hears a vehicle and sees Sir Patrick driving the pony-chaise back from the station alone, without Duncan. Sir Patrick stops, confirms that Arnold knows the matter is secret, and asks whether anything has happened.
